app:
Every run publishes one app over all the modules that ran: `https://OWNER.github.io/REPO/` once GitHub Pages serves the
`stackvitals-data` branch. For a private repo, `stackvitals ui owner/repo` opens the same app on `127.0.0.1` from a copy
of that branch. The app is `docs/index.html` plus `docs/app/` in the branch: Preact and TypeScript bundled ahead of
time, with its font, the docs for Help and the demo data inside. It loads no code from other sites (apart from the SQL
explorer, which fetches DuckDB once) and has no tracking. The bundled libraries and their licences are listed in
`app/LICENSES.md`.

## Opening it

| Address | What opens |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | The repo whose data sits beside the page (the usual Pages site) |
| `index.html?demo=1` | The demo: three example repos with full data, nothing to connect |
| `index.html?repo=owner/name` | A repo's `stackvitals-data` branch, read from GitHub |
| `index.html?pages=https://owner.github.io/name/` | Another repo's Pages site |
| `index.html?welcome` | The Welcome screen |


## Layout

The sidebar groups the pages: **Health** (Overview, Insights, CI Health, Pull Requests, Delivery, Community,
Dependencies), **Organisation** (Investment, Portal, Explore), **Team** (Activity, Data health, Settings) and **Install** (Setup,
Connections, Agents, Help, About). A badge shows what waits on a page, for example flaky tests or newcomers waiting. A
page for a module that isn't set up is dimmed. On a phone the sidebar becomes a tab bar (Overview, Insights, CI, PRs)
with the rest under **More**.

The top bar holds the repo switcher: the repos you follow, **Add a repository** (by name or Pages address), your GitHub
repos, the demo, reloading the data, and appearance (light, dark or auto).

## First run

Where no repo's data sits beside the page (the project site, or a fresh install), the app opens on **Welcome** with three
choices:

1. **Connect GitHub.** Lists your repos: ones that run StackVitals open their dashboard, the others go to Setup.
2. **Try the demo.** Three example repos with full data.
3. **Open a public repo.** Type `owner/repo`; the app reads its published data from its Pages site or data branch, or
   offers setup when it has none.

A returning visitor with a remembered connection goes straight to the last repo.

## Connecting GitHub

- **With a token.** The app opens GitHub's token page with the name, a 90-day expiry and the permissions filled in; you
  pick the repos and paste the token back. It is checked at once, and the app lists what it can and can't do in plain
  words. The token goes only to `api.github.com`. It stays in this tab by default; switch on **Remember on this device**
  to keep it across visits. **Sign out** forgets it.
- **Sign in with GitHub.** Shown only when the site was built with a sign-in relay (`worker/relay`). The app uses
  GitHub's sign-in with PKCE; the relay only swaps the one-time code (and later a refresh) for a token and keeps
  nothing. A signed-in token lasts 8 hours and is renewed shortly before.

## Setup in a few clicks

Once GitHub is connected, setup takes a few clicks; connecting takes one token, made from a prefilled GitHub page.
**Setup** picks a repo, checks what it has and suggests a plan (modules ticked from what it finds) that you can change.
**Set it up** then commits the workflow (a pull request when the branch is protected), starts the first run and shows it
live, waits for the data branch and turns on Pages for public repos. Each step is saved, so a reload picks up where it
stopped. Without a token you get the file ready to add on GitHub, the YAML to copy, or the one CLI command (`stackvitals init owner/repo`), and the app
checks for the first run at a pace that stays inside GitHub's limit for visitors.

## Pages

| Page | What it shows | What you can do there |
|---|---|---|
| Overview | Installation health, the state of each area, the trend you pick, what needs a decision, what to fix first and decisions ending soon | Open any item |
| Insights | Every finding ranked by the hours at stake, with its sample, evidence, age and decision; flaky tests traced to the pull requests they held red | Snooze or acknowledge; query it in Explore |
| CI Health | The first-try green share with the pushes that missed it, flaky and failing tests and jobs by cost, failure groups (each with a prompt to copy into an AI agent), slowest tests and jobs, new and skipped tests, coverage; a page per item with its flake rate, the runs that show it and the decision in force | Quarantine (tests), mute, acknowledge, reopen |
| Pull Requests | Who holds the next move on each open pull request, stuck ones, working-agreement exceptions | Filter to your handle; leave a pull request out of the numbers |
| Delivery | DORA tiles with tiers (each opens into the deployments, pull requests and incidents it was counted from), deployment rework rate, the phases of a change and their trend, AI-assisted work, issues and sprints with Jira or Linear, the merge queue | Open the pull requests behind each phase and each DORA number |
| Community | Newcomers waiting for an answer, bus factor (no names), first answers for newcomers against regulars, stars and traffic | |
| Dependencies | Vulnerabilities and malware in every lockfile the scanner reads, runtimes out of support, update pull requests by age, the supply chain from the SBOM | Accept a risk or a licence until a date |
| Investment | Where merged work went each month (feature, fix, maintenance, security, docs) and how each pull request was sorted | |
| Portal | (portal repos) every repo with its level, owners and links; failing rules; the catalog; campaigns; golden paths | Open a repo's own app |
| Explore | The tables behind every page, one row per pull request, job, test or deployment | Download any table; open the SQL explorer (`explore.html`, DuckDB in your browser) |
| Activity | Every decision and settings change: who, when, why, until when | Undo in one click |
| Data health | Each source (every step of the run, every connected service): current, filling in, failing since when and why, when it last worked, what it read; how far back each history goes against how long it is kept, and what retention or the size cap last removed | |
| Settings | Every setting in groups, with its default, the value in force and what a change would do | Change settings and send them |
| Setup | Setup in a few clicks (above) | |
| Connections | Everything StackVitals reads or sends (GitHub, Jira, Linear, chat webhooks, other CI systems, DevLake), grouped as connected, needs attention or available | Save a secret, change its settings, test it |
| Agents | Connecting a coding agent to the MCP server, one config per client; the tools by module, the skills | Copy the config or the install command |
| Help | The StackVitals docs, with search; links between docs stay in the app | |
| About | The path from GitHub to this page, where the data lives, how numbers are counted, how accurate each rule is, what each permission is for, how to remove it all | |

## Where a number comes from

The headline numbers open into what they were counted from: deployment frequency into the deployments, lead time into each deployed pull request with its time (longest first), change fail rate into the deployments and the revert, hotfix or incident issue tied to each, recovery into each failed deployment and its time to resolve, every review phase into its pull requests, and the first-try green share into the pushes that missed it, each linked to GitHub. The same lists are in `delivery.json` and `data.json` (`evidence`, `not_first_try`), and the MCP tools return them, so an agent can answer "why is lead time 26 hours?" with the pull requests. Long lists keep the longest or newest first and say the total. From a terminal: `stackvitals explain owner/repo lead-time` (or `deployments`, `change-failure`, `recovery`, `first-try`, or a review phase like `pickup`) prints the number, what it means and each item with its GitHub link; `--json` for all of them.

## Data health

Every run writes `health.json` beside the other files: for each step of the run and each connected service, when it
last worked, whether it is failing and since when (with what it said), whether it has finished reading its history
(**Filling in** while a big history is read a few hundred items a run, within GitHub's and the service's limits), and
what it read. It also lists how far back each kind of history goes against how long it is kept, and what retention or
the size cap last removed, so a gap in a chart has a reason. A failing source keeps its last good data and the next
run tries again; a source with no run for two days may mean the schedule stopped (GitHub pauses schedules in repos
with no activity for 60 days). Times and counts refresh with the next run that changes something, so a quiet run
never commits just to move a clock.

## Connections

Each connection opens a sheet with what it unlocks, the steps, its secrets and its settings. A secret you type is sealed
in your browser with the repo's own public key and only the sealed value goes to GitHub, the same way GitHub's own
settings page saves it; the app can list secret names but never read a value back. **Test connection** starts the
workflow's check and reads the result back from `connectors.json`. For Linear the app can also test the key straight
from the page; the key then goes only to `api.linear.app`.

## Making a decision

"Decide" on a test, job, finding or pull request asks what to do, for how long and why. Quarantine and mute last 30
days, snooze 14, an accepted risk 30, unless you pick another length or a date. Then pick how it reaches the repo:

1. **Open the request on GitHub** (the default). A prefilled issue opens; press Submit. The workflow checks you have
   triage access or more, records the decision, answers and closes the issue. No token is involved.
2. **Apply now** with your connected GitHub account or a pasted token with **Actions: read and write**: the app starts the
   workflow with the request and shows the run.
3. **Copy as a comment.** The command to paste in any issue or pull request comment, for example
   `/stackvitals mute test:<id> for 7d because <reason>`.

Decisions land in `decisions/log.ndjson` on the data branch and show in Activity. Issues from people without access
start no run.

## Changing settings

Edits collect in a save bar. **Review** lists each change (old to new); for alert thresholds it replays the last 90 days
and says how often the new value would have fired. With GitHub connected, one click commits `.github/stackvitals.toml`
(a pull request when the branch is protected) or runs the workflow with the request; workflow inputs are edited in the
workflow file the same way. Without a connection, open a prefilled issue or copy the TOML. Settings need write access.

## On this device

The app keeps your repo list, theme and GitHub handle in this browser only. A token stays in this tab unless you
ask to remember it on this device.

## For agents

`stackvitals propose owner/repo --set KEY=VALUE --decide "/stackvitals ..."` (MCP: `propose_change`) prints the same
prefilled request link, checked with the workflow's own parsers. A person opens it and presses Submit.
faq:
## Is it really free? What's the catch?

It is licensed under Apache 2.0 and runs in your own GitHub Actions minutes, which are free for public repos and included in every
plan for private ones. There is no paid tier, no account and no StackVitals-hosted backend.
Optional integrations (a tracker, chat, a model for triage, storage outside git) use services and keys you choose, under
their own terms ([governance](../GOVERNANCE.md)).

## Does my code or data leave GitHub?

History is files on a branch of your repo, and your code is never sent anywhere. By default the dependency check
sends your dependencies' package names to deps.dev, OpenSSF Scorecard and the registries' download counts; set
`[deps] outside_lookups = false` to keep them in GitHub. Explore and the printable pages load their libraries from
public CDNs. Anything else (your Jira, your chat) needs a key you add. Each host and what it gets is listed on
[privacy](privacy.md).

## How many Actions minutes does it use?

A run takes about a minute on a small repo. It starts after your CI workflows and every 3 hours, so a busy repo runs
it often; on private repos, check that against your plan's minutes. For the busiest public repos (2,000 CI runs a
day), CI Health alone is estimated at under 40% of the built-in token's API limit ([scaling](scaling.md)).

## How is this different from asking an AI agent to look at my CI?

An agent with GitHub access sees what GitHub still has: 90 days of logs and whatever it can read in one chat.
StackVitals keeps the history after GitHub deletes it, has already counted how often each test flaked, and compares
your repo with similar public ones from a daily crawl. On a single fresh failure a good agent does as well alone; we
measured that and say so ([agents card](../bench/accuracy/agents/README.md)). The two work together: the MCP server
gives agents StackVitals' history.

## How is it different from LinearB, Swarmia, Trunk or DevLake?

They are good tools, and each does some things better; [docs/compare](compare/README.md) has a page per tool (DevLake,
Middleware, CDviz, Pelorus, Liatrio's Backstage plugin, Faros, GrimoireLab, LinearB, Swarmia, Trunk and BuildPulse)
saying where, with sources. StackVitals differs in three ways: it is free and has no hosted backend; the rules behind
its verdicts and headline numbers are checked on public data with the losses published ([accuracy](accuracy.md)); and it
compares like with like (the same repo, month and size) before saying something changed. Where we ran another tool on
the same repos (DevLake and Middleware), the results are on the cards, including where theirs tie or beat ours.

## Can it rate developers?

No. People are named only to route work (an owner, who acts next on a pull request). The [DORA guide](dora-guide.md)
explains why team numbers must never be used for individual reviews.

## Why does it say "not enough data" so often?

Because a number from three pull requests misleads. Each figure shows its sample size, and below a floor it says so
instead of guessing. Small repos borrow strength from similar repos where that has been checked to help.

## A verdict was wrong. What do I do?

Say so with `/stackvitals dispute test:<id> because <why>` (or `confirm` when it was right). It is recorded with who
and why, and CI Health shows how often your team confirmed each kind of verdict. If the run is public, an issue with
its link helps the next accuracy check.

## Does it work with GitLab, Jenkins or Buildkite?

GitLab CI: a job you include in `.gitlab-ci.yml` keeps the pipeline history, publishes CI Health on GitLab Pages and
notes failed merge requests (preview; [connectors](connectors.md#gitlab)). Test reports from Jenkins, CircleCI and
Buildkite can be uploaded with `stackvitals ci upload`. Everything else reads GitHub ([connectors](connectors.md), [limitations](limitations.md)).

## Does it work on GitHub Enterprise Server?

The Action reads the API and GraphQL addresses GitHub Actions gives every job (`GITHUB_API_URL`,
`GITHUB_GRAPHQL_URL`), so on GitHub Enterprise Server it talks to your server, not github.com. Two limits: links in
the app point to github.com pages, and the daily crawl's peer comparisons cover public github.com repos only. The
command line takes the same two variables when you run it against your server.

## Is there a login, with roles for who sees what?

Yes, and it is GitHub's own. The app uses your GitHub token (or GitHub sign-in, where the site has a sign-in relay) and reads each repo's data branch with your access, so a
person sees exactly the repos GitHub already lets them read, and an org's roles (members, outside collaborators, teams)
apply unchanged; Portal's org view shows only the repos the viewer can open. Nothing is copied to a server of ours to
guard, so there is no second user list to keep in step. What you don't get is a separate admin screen for roles: you
manage them where you already do, in GitHub.

## Our repos are private. Can we still see the dashboard?

Yes, three ways. Run `stackvitals ui OWNER/REPO` to open it on your machine. Set `pages: artifact`: each run that
changed the app uploads it as a download kept 7 days; unzip it and run `python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1`
in the folder (opening `index.html` directly doesn't work). Or use Pages if your plan keeps Pages private
([enterprise](enterprise.md)).

## What happens if a run fails halfway?

Nothing is half-written: each run commits once, and the next run catches up. The tested failure modes are listed in
[limitations](limitations.md#failure-modes).
install:
StackVitals has two parts: a GitHub Action, `uses: stackvitals/stackvitals@v0`, that runs in your repo, and the `stackvitals` command on your machine, which sets the Action up, opens a private repo's dashboard and runs the MCP server for AI agents. The Action needs nothing installed; the command is one `pip install`.

## Get the command

```sh
pip install stackvitals      # Python 3.11 or newer
gh auth login                # once; or set GITHUB_TOKEN
```

Or run any command without installing, with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/): `uvx stackvitals init owner/repo`. Upgrade with `pip install -U stackvitals`. `stackvitals sql` needs the SQL extra: `pip install "stackvitals[sql]"`. The same package holds the CLI, `stackvitals ui` (a dashboard on your machine) and the MCP server (`stackvitals serve`).

## Set up a repo

```sh
stackvitals init owner/repo
```

`init` commits the workflow file below (or opens a pull request when the branch is protected or a different `stackvitals.yml` is there), follows the first run and turns on GitHub Pages for a public repo. A private repo keeps Pages off, since a Pages site is public on most plans: open its dashboard with `stackvitals ui owner/repo`. The app's Setup page does the same without a terminal. More: [quickstart.md](quickstart.md).

`stackvitals/stackvitals@v0` follows the latest release; to pin an exact one, use its version tag (`stackvitals/stackvitals@vX.Y.Z`, listed under [releases](https://github.com/stackvitals/stackvitals/releases)).

The rest of this page is the reference for doing it by hand. The file below is exactly what `stackvitals ci init owner/repo` prints (that command also fills in your CI workflows' names) and what `init` and the app's Setup page commit for you. Save it as `.github/workflows/stackvitals.yml`; committing it starts the first run. No settings file is needed: a missing `.github/stackvitals.toml` means the defaults ([settings.md](settings.md)).

## Modules

Pick modules with the `modules` input, comma separated. To run one alone, list only it, for example `modules: ci`. Delivery and Insights have no id of their own: they come with `flow`.

| Id | What you get | Runs on | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ci` | CI Health: flaky and slowing jobs and tests, the PR verdict comment and check, test reports, owners | after each CI run finishes, and every 3 hours | nothing; alone is fine |
| `flow` | Team Flow, and with it the Delivery page (cycle time, DORA, AI-assisted work, investment) and Insights (fix first, alerts, the weekly digest) | the schedule and manual runs | nothing; Delivery's CI parts (failed deployments from CI, merge-queue flakes) and Insights' red-CI findings also need `ci` |
| `deps` | Dependency Steward: known vulnerabilities and malware in every lockfile, the check on PRs that change a lockfile, runtimes, and the weekly supply chain page | after each CI run (with `ci`) and every 3 hours for vulnerabilities; pull requests that change a lockfile; weekly for the supply chain | nothing; alone is fine |
| `community` | Community: newcomers, first answers, who carries the work, stars and traffic | the schedule and manual runs | nothing; it reads the PRs itself when `flow` isn't on |
| `portal` | Portal: the org's catalog, owners and scorecards | the schedule, from the org's portal repo with its own workflow (below) | a portal repo; an org App for private repos |

The default is `ci,flow,deps,community`. `stackvitals ci init --modules ci,deps` (or the app's Setup picker) writes a file with only those modules' triggers and permissions, each lowered to read where nothing of theirs writes; turning on a writing switch later (like `deps-comments`, which needs `pull-requests: write`) means raising that permission too.

## The workflow file

Change `workflows: ["CI"]` to the `name:` lines of your CI workflows (the names, not the file names): `workflow_run` matches names. The permissions are what every default switch needs; each comment says what to lower to turn a part off. Team Flow's automation (review requests, size labels) and PR comments need `pull-requests: write`; the weekly digest, commands and flaky-test issues need `issues: write`. A settings change applied from the app opens a pull request, which needs the repo setting "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" (Settings, Actions, General).

```yaml
name: StackVitals
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["CI"]   # your CI workflows; each finished run is read right away
    types: [completed]
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 */3 * * *"   # Team Flow every 3 hours, and a CI catch-up
  repository_dispatch:
    types: [stackvitals-deployment, stackvitals-incident]   # sent by `stackvitals record` from any deploy tool
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      request:
        description: "A change sent from the StackVitals app (leave empty for a normal run)"
        required: false
        default: ""
  push:                      # your settings file applies at once; adding this file starts the first run
    paths: [".github/stackvitals.toml", ".github/workflows/stackvitals.yml"]
  issues:
    types: [opened, closed, reopened]  # requests from the app; flaky-test issues closed as not planned, or reopened
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]         # /stackvitals commands
  pull_request:              # the dependency check, only when a lockfile changes (never runs the PR's code)
    paths: ["**/*.lock", "**/*lock.json", "**/*lock.yaml", "**/npm-shrinkwrap.json", "**/requirements*.txt", "**/go.mod",
            "**/*.lockfile", "**/pom.xml", "**/pylock*.toml", "**/Package.resolved", "**/gems.locked",
            "**/verification-metadata.xml", "**/*.freeze"]
permissions:
  contents: write        # saves history to the stackvitals-data branch; settings changes asked for from the app
  actions: read          # reads your CI runs, jobs and test reports (write: [automation] rerun_flaky re-runs known flakes)
  checks: read           # Team Flow: sees which PRs have failing checks (write: [automation] verdict_check)
  statuses: read
  deployments: read      # Team Flow: delivery from deployments
  issues: write          # the weekly digest, answers to /stackvitals commands, flaky-test and alert issues
  pull-requests: write   # reads PRs for Team Flow; one comment on failed PR runs (set to read to turn comments off)
jobs:
  vitals:
    # Only what concerns StackVitals starts a runner: settings pushed to the default branch, requests and commands from
    # people with access to the repo, and flaky-test issues being closed or reopened.
    if: >-
      (github.event_name != 'push' || github.ref_name == github.event.repository.default_branch) &&
      (github.event_name != 'issues' ||
        (github.event.action == 'opened' && contains(github.event.issue.body, '```stackvitals') &&
         contains(fromJSON('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.issue.author_association)) ||
        (github.event.action != 'opened' && contains(github.event.issue.labels.*.name, 'flaky-test'))) &&
      (github.event_name != 'issue_comment' ||
        (contains(github.event.comment.body, '/stackvitals') &&
         contains(fromJSON('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association))) &&
      (github.event_name != 'workflow_run' || !github.event.repository.private ||
        github.event.workflow_run.conclusion != 'success' || vars.STACKVITALS_EVERY_CI_RUN == 'true')
    # Private repos pay for Actions minutes: a CI run that passed starts no job (the 3-hourly run reads it), unless the
    # repo variable STACKVITALS_EVERY_CI_RUN is "true" (the verdict check needs it). On the job, so events it skips never
    # wait in (or cancel) the queue; PR checks and Test connection runs never wait for (or get dropped behind) data runs.
    concurrency:
      group: stackvitals-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || (contains(github.event.inputs.request, '"check"') && format('check-{0}', github.run_id)) || 'data' }}
      cancel-in-progress: false
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: stackvitals/stackvitals@v0
        env:
          STACKVITALS_EVERY_CI_RUN: ${{ vars.STACKVITALS_EVERY_CI_RUN }}
        with:
          modules: ci,flow,deps,community
          jira-email: ${{ secrets.JIRA_EMAIL }}        # optional: Jira Cloud (see Integrations); unused while unset
          jira-token: ${{ secrets.JIRA_API_TOKEN }}
          linear-token: ${{ secrets.LINEAR_API_KEY }}  # optional: Linear
          pagerduty-token: ${{ secrets.PAGERDUTY_API_KEY }}       # optional: PagerDuty or incident.io incidents
          incident-io-token: ${{ secrets.INCIDENT_IO_API_KEY }}
          triage-key: ${{ secrets.GEMINI_API_KEY }}     # optional: a model's view on undecided failures ([ci.triage])
          # traffic-token: ${{ steps.app.outputs.token }}   # optional: keep traffic past GitHub's 14 days (see docs/modules.md)
```

## The portal workflow

Portal runs in the org's own portal repo (private is best) with this file, which `stackvitals portal init` prints; `stackvitals portal check ORG` says what your token can read first.

```yaml
name: StackVitals Portal
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "41 5 * * *"   # once a day
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      request:
        description: "A request from the StackVitals app, like a golden path (leave empty for a normal run)"
        required: false
        default: ""
  issues:
    types: [opened]          # golden path requests from the app, run at once
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]         # "/stackvitals approve" on a golden path that needs an approval
permissions:
  contents: write          # keeps the catalog, its history and the pages in this repo's stackvitals-data branch
  issues: write            # one tracking issue per campaign, and answers to requests, in this repo only
concurrency:
  group: stackvitals-portal
  cancel-in-progress: false
jobs:
  portal:
    # Request issues start a run only when someone with access to this repo opened one with a StackVitals block.
    if: >-
      (github.event_name != 'issues' ||
       (contains(github.event.issue.body, '```stackvitals') &&
        contains(fromJSON('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.issue.author_association))) &&
      (github.event_name != 'issue_comment' ||
       (startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '/stackvitals approve') &&
        contains(fromJSON('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association)))
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      # Private repos: create an org-owned read-only GitHub App (see docs/modules.md), store its client ID and key, then switch on.
      # - uses: actions/create-github-app-token@64ab729a6294000f5aa4a4bc0b73d1f32bc45510 # v3
      #   id: app
      #   with:
      #     client-id: ${{ vars.PORTAL_CLIENT_ID }}
      #     private-key: ${{ secrets.PORTAL_PRIVATE_KEY }}
      #     owner: ${{ github.repository_owner }}
      - uses: stackvitals/stackvitals@v0
        with:
          modules: portal
          # portal-token: ${{ steps.app.outputs.token }}
```

## Every input

From [action.yml](https://github.com/stackvitals/stackvitals/blob/main/action.yml). Inputs use hyphens (`rerun-flaky`); the same switches in `.github/stackvitals.toml` use underscores (`rerun_flaky`), and the file wins when both are set.

| Input | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `modules` | `ci,flow,deps,community` | Modules to run, comma separated. Available now - ci (CI health), flow (Team Flow, on schedule and manual runs), deps (dependency check on pull requests that change a lockfile), community (newcomers, first answers, stars and traffic, on schedule and manual runs), portal (the org catalog, run from the org's private portal repo) |
| `token` | `${{ github.token }}` | Token that can read Actions and write the stackvitals-data branch |
| `portal-token` |  | Optional token from an org-owned read-only GitHub App, so Portal reads the org's private repos (without it, public repos only) |
| `portal-org` |  | The org Portal catalogs (default - the owner of the repo it runs in) |
| `traffic-token` |  | Optional token from your own GitHub App with Administration read, so Community keeps traffic past GitHub's 14 days (the built-in token can't read traffic) |
| `days` | `90` | Days of history to fill in on the first runs (GitHub keeps at most 90) |
| `budget` | `800` | Most API requests per run (the built-in token allows 1,000 an hour) |
| `tests` | `true` | Read test reports (JUnit XML or CTRF JSON) from your run artifacts to find single flaky tests |
| `test-artifacts` |  | Regex for the artifact names that hold test reports (empty = names with junit, test-results, ctrf...) |
| `pr-comments` | `true` | One comment on failed PR runs saying which failures are known flakes (needs pull-requests write) |
| `rerun-flaky` | `false` | Re-run failed jobs once when every failure is a known flake (needs actions write) |
| `quarantine` | `false` | Keep a list of flaky tests for the stackvitals ci quarantine command |
| `preflight-comments` | `false` | Team Flow - one note on new outside PRs that miss what merged PRs here usually include (needs pull-requests write) |
| `deps-comments` | `false` | Dependency check - one comment on same-repo PRs listing changed packages and their verdicts (needs pull-requests write) |
| `issues` | `false` | Keep one issue per flaky test or job, closed once fixed (needs issues write) |
| `mention-owners` | `false` | @-mention a flaky test's code owners in the issues StackVitals opens (off: owners are named without a notification) |
| `webhook` |  | Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams (Workflows) or any JSON webhook URL (pass a secret) to hear when something newly turns flaky and when a delivery number crosses its threshold |
| `team-webhooks` |  | One "@org/team = https://..." line per team (pass a secret); a team's newly flaky tests go to its own chat, the rest to webhook |
| `jira-email` |  | The Jira Cloud account's email (pass a secret); with jira-token and [connectors.jira] url, issues, sprints and incidents are read |
| `jira-token` |  | A Jira Cloud API token for that account (pass a secret; it expires within a year, so set key_expires to be warned) |
| `linear-token` |  | A Linear personal API key (pass a secret); issues and cycles of the teams under [connectors.linear] are read |
| `pagerduty-token` |  | A PagerDuty REST API key, read-only (pass a secret); its incidents then count in DORA instead of labels, reverts and hotfixes |
| `incident-io-token` |  | An incident.io API key with read access (pass a secret); its incidents then count in DORA instead of labels, reverts and hotfixes |
| `sonar-token` |  | A SonarQube or SonarCloud token (pass a secret), only for a private project or your own server; public SonarCloud projects need none |
| `copilot-token` |  | A token that can read the org's Copilot usage reports (an org App with "Organization Copilot metrics" read, or a fine-grained token); kept day by day |
| `anthropic-admin-key` |  | An Anthropic Admin API key (sk-ant-admin..., pass a secret); the organisation's daily Claude API cost is set beside AI-involved pull requests |
| `openai-admin-key` |  | An OpenAI admin key (pass a secret); the organisation's daily API cost is set beside AI-involved pull requests |
| `cursor-admin-key` |  | A Cursor admin API key (pass a secret); the team's billing-cycle spend and daily agent use are set beside AI-involved pull requests |
| `slack-token` |  | A Slack bot token (channels:history) that reads the support channels under [connectors.slack]; only times and flags are kept |
| `discord-token` |  | A Discord bot token (View Channel, Read Message History) that reads the support channels under [connectors.discord]; only times and flags are kept |
| `imports-json` |  | Path to the list of packages your code imports (`stackvitals deps imports --out imports.json` in an earlier step, after checkout) for Python, JavaScript and Rust repos; known vulnerabilities then say whether your code imports the package (an import, not a call path) |
| `govulncheck-json` |  | Path to govulncheck's JSON output (`govulncheck -format json ./... > govulncheck.json` in an earlier step) for Go repos; the supply page then says which advisories the code really calls |
| `triage-key` |  | A model API key (pass a secret, e.g. a free Gemini key from Google AI Studio) for [ci.triage]; up to 3 undecided failures per run get a model's view beside the verdict |
| `label-stuck` | `false` | Label pull requests whose asked-for review has not started after 3 days ("stackvitals: waiting for review"), and take the label off once one has (needs pull-requests or issues write) |
| `retention-days` | `400` | Days of pull request, issue and Portal history kept in the data branch |
| `ci-retention-days` | `180` | Days of CI run and test history kept in the data branch |
| `size-cap-mb` | `250` | Most history kept in the data branch, in MB; the oldest days go first |
| `squash-history` | `false` | Every 1,000 commits, rewrite the data branch to one commit (files unchanged; the branch is force-pushed) |
| `pages` | `branch` | "branch" (default): GitHub Pages serves the stackvitals-data branch. "deploy": this job publishes the monitor itself (Pages source "GitHub Actions"; the job needs pages and id-token write and the github-pages environment), for busy repos past 10 Pages builds an hour. "artifact": no Pages; each run that changed the app uploads it as a workflow artifact (kept 7 days, or less if your org sets a shorter limit) to download and open locally, for private repos; anyone who can read the repo can download it |
| `storage` | `git` | Where history is kept: "git" (default, the stackvitals-data branch) or an S3-compatible bucket as s3://bucket/prefix (AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO: the service must support replace-only-if-unchanged writes, If-Match), for very busy repos and big orgs. Switching starts a fresh history (the branch is not copied). With a bucket, publish the app with pages "deploy" or "artifact"; the tools that read the stackvitals-data branch (stackvitals ui and sql, Explore, the MCP server, the Portal org view, quarantine in your CI) do not read a bucket yet |
| `s3-endpoint` |  | The bucket service's endpoint, like https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com or https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com |
| `s3-region` | `auto` | The bucket's region ("auto" for R2) |
| `s3-key-id` |  | An access key id that can read, write, delete and list that prefix (pass a secret) |
| `s3-secret` |  | Its secret (pass a secret) |
quickstart:
A GitHub repo is all you need; CI on GitHub Actions makes the CI part useful. There are three ways to set it up:

- **One command** (fastest): `stackvitals init OWNER/REPO`, just below.
- **No terminal:** the StackVitals app's Setup page checks your repo and, with a GitHub token, commits the workflow, starts the first run and turns on Pages (public repos only). Connecting takes one token, made from a prefilled GitHub page; without a token it opens GitHub with the file ready.
- **By hand:** steps 1 to 3 below.

A public repo gets its monitor on GitHub Pages. A private repo works the same way, but you open its monitor on your machine or as a download (step 3), because Pages from a private repo is public on most plans.

## The one-command way

```
pip install stackvitals
gh auth login
stackvitals init OWNER/REPO
```

`init` does steps 1 to 3 below for you: it commits the workflow (or opens a pull request when the branch is protected or
a different `stackvitals.yml` is there), follows the first run, checks the `stackvitals-data` branch and turns on Pages
for a public repo. A private repo keeps Pages off, since a Pages site is public on most plans; open its dashboard with
`stackvitals ui OWNER/REPO`. `--no-wait` returns once the first run has started; run `init` again to finish. The steps
below are the same, by hand.

## 1. Add the workflow

Print a workflow that already names your CI workflows, and save it in your repo:

```
stackvitals ci init OWNER/REPO > .github/workflows/stackvitals.yml
```

(After `pip install stackvitals`; or put `uvx` in front to run it without installing, with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).)

It runs CI health, Team Flow, the dependency check and Community, and starts after the CI workflows it names (the ones that look like tests and builds; edit the list as you like). To install only some modules, print the file for them, for example `uvx stackvitals ci init OWNER/REPO --modules ci,deps`: it asks only for the permissions and triggers those modules use (the app's Setup page has the same choice). Every permission in the file has a comment saying what it is for. The whole file, what each module id needs and every input: [install.md](install.md).

## 2. Commit it

Commit the file to your default branch. That starts the first run by itself (it also runs after every CI run and every 3 hours; on a private repo a CI run that passed waits for the 3-hourly run, unless the repo variable `STACKVITALS_EVERY_CI_RUN` is `true`). The first run reads up to 90 days of CI history and a year of pull requests; on a small repo it finished 55 seconds after the commit, and on a busy repo it may say "still filling in older history", and the next runs continue where it stopped. The supply chain part needs GitHub's dependency graph (on for public repos; for a private repo turn it on under Settings, Code security); until then the job says so once a week.

## 3. Turn on the dashboard

Open **Settings → Pages**. Under "Build and deployment", choose **Deploy from a branch**, branch `stackvitals-data`, folder `/docs`, and save. After a minute the dashboard is at:

```
https://OWNER.github.io/REPO/
```

That address opens the StackVitals app: Overview first, then a page per module, Settings (change any setting and save it with your GitHub token, or send it as an issue the workflow applies), Activity (every decision and change), Connections and Help. Add `?demo=1` to the address for three example repos; [app.md](app.md) walks through it. The module pages (`ci.html`, `flow.html`, ...) stay as printable views and work without JavaScript.

**A private repo:** skip Pages and run `pip install stackvitals` then `stackvitals ui OWNER/REPO` (it uses your `gh` login or `GITHUB_TOKEN` for one git command and keeps nothing). The same app opens on `127.0.0.1` in a few seconds.

**No workflow in the repo:** after `pip install stackvitals` and `gh auth login`, `stackvitals ui OWNER/REPO --collect` reads a repo's history on your machine (CI runs and pull requests, 90 days by default) into a local data branch and opens the app, with no Action, server, database or Docker. It only reads from GitHub: nothing is posted, labelled or committed there. On pallets/click the first read took 11 minutes.

## What next

- **Single flaky tests:** upload your test results (JUnit XML, CTRF, Jest or Vitest JSON, `go test -json`, .NET TRX) with `actions/upload-artifact` under a name containing `test-results`, `junit` or `ctrf`.
- **Opt-in automation:** turn switches on under `[automation]` in `.github/stackvitals.toml` (`rerun_flaky`, `issues`, `assign_owners`, `mention_owners`, `quarantine`, `preflight_comments`, `deps_comments`, `label_stuck`), or with the Action input of the same name written with hyphens (`rerun-flaky`; the file wins when both are set); [docs/settings.md](settings.md) lists every setting and the permission each needs. The `webhook` input takes a Slack, Discord, Teams or JSON URL.
- **Traffic history:** pass a token from your own GitHub App as `traffic-token:` (see [Community](modules.md#community)).
- **Your org:** Portal runs from a separate private repo (`stackvitals portal init`).
- **Workflow inputs** (like `pages: artifact` or `webhook:`) go under `with:` in the StackVitals step of `.github/workflows/stackvitals.yml`; every input is in [install.md](install.md#every-input).
- **Agents:** `stackvitals serve` starts the MCP server (in Claude Code: `claude mcp add stackvitals -- uvx stackvitals serve`; other clients: [the README](../README.md#ai-agents-mcp)); `stackvitals contribute brief OWNER/REPO` prints how changes get merged in a repo.
- **Busy repos:** GitHub Pages builds a branch about 10 times an hour at most. Past that, publish from the job instead: set `pages: deploy` on the Action, choose **GitHub Actions** as the Pages source, and give the job `pages: write`, `id-token: write` and `environment: github-pages`.

## If something goes wrong

- **"Resource not accessible by integration":** a permission is missing from the workflow file; the job summary names it.
- **No dashboard after enabling Pages:** check that the `stackvitals-data` branch exists (it is created by the first run) and that Pages points at its `/docs` folder.
- **Private repos:** GitHub Pages from a private repo is public on most plans, so set `pages: artifact` (each run that changed the app uploads it as a download kept 7 days; unzip it and follow its OPEN-ME.txt), or use `stackvitals ui OWNER/REPO` on your machine instead.
guides-maintainer:
You want red CI to stop eating contributors' time, newcomers answered, and fewer surprise dependency breaks. The Action
is free on public repos and needs only the built-in token.

## Set it up

[Quickstart](../quickstart.md): `stackvitals init owner/repo` adds the workflow file, runs it once and turns on GitHub Pages from the `stackvitals-data` branch. Your
dashboard is public like your repo. Your code stays in GitHub; the dependency check sends package names to deps.dev
and the registries unless you set `[deps] outside_lookups = false` ([privacy](../privacy.md)).

## CI that contributors can trust

- When CI fails on a pull request, one comment says which failures are known flakes, which already fail on the
  default branch and which are likely the change's own ([modules](../modules.md#ci-health)). The verdict check still
  blocks until CI is green, so a flake is re-run, never waved through.
- Upload test reports (JUnit XML, CTRF, Jest, Vitest, `go test -json`, TRX) to see single flaky tests, not just jobs.
- Opt in under `[automation]` to re-run known flakes once, open one issue per flaky test, or quarantine one.
- Contributors and agents can ask `stackvitals contribute brief owner/repo` for how changes get merged here: what
  merged pull requests usually include, who reviews each folder, and which tests are flaky.

## Newcomers

Community shows how fast issues get a first answer from the project (maintainers, regular responders and triagers;
drive-by comments don't count), where newcomers drop out, and who carries the work
([modules](../modules.md#community)). Issues still waiting stay in the median, so a slow week can't hide.

## Dependencies

On each pull request that changes a lockfile, the Dependency Steward checks what was added or upgraded: advisories on
the installed version, look-alike names, licence changes, and how the same upgrade went in other public repos
([modules](../modules.md#dependency-steward)).

## Commands

Anyone with triage access can decide from a comment: `/stackvitals acknowledge`, `mute`, `snooze`, `quarantine`, `accept` and more, with `for 14d` and
`because <reason>`. Every decision is recorded with who and why, and temporary ones end on their own ([all commands](../modules.md#decide-on-github-hear-back-every-week)).
guides-manager:
You want to know where your team's time goes and whether changes help, without rating people. This is the path.

## First week

1. **Set it up** on each of your team's repos ([quickstart](../quickstart.md)), or on one repo first. It reads up to
   90 days of CI and a year of pull requests on the first run, so you start with history, not an empty page.
2. **Open Insights** in the app: one list of what to fix first across CI, reviews and delivery, ranked by hours at
   stake ([modules](../modules.md#insights-what-to-fix-first)). Start at the top.
3. **Read Delivery** for cycle time in LinearB's phases (coding, pickup, review, deploy) and DORA's five metrics (the industry's standard delivery measures: how often you deploy, how long a change takes to ship, how often a change fails, and how fast you recover). Before you share a DORA number,
   read [the DORA guide](../dora-guide.md): what each number can't tell, how it gets gamed, and why it is never for
   individual reviews.

## Every week

- The **weekly digest** (Monday, one comment on a pinned issue; to post it to chat too, set the `webhook` input, then `channels = ["issue", "webhook"]` under `[digest]`) says what
  changed. It reports a change only when it stands out from how much your repo's weeks usually swing, so false alarms
  are rare, but a quiet digest means nothing stood out, not that nothing moved: on small repos even large slowdowns
  can go unflagged ([modules](../modules.md#decide-on-github-hear-back-every-week)).
- **Working agreements** you set under `[agreements]` (first review within a day, PRs under 400 lines) are previewed
  week by week before you turn them on, then counted in the digest.
- The digest asks three **pulse** questions by reaction; StackVitals shows only the counts (GitHub itself shows who
  reacted to anyone who can see the issue).

## Questions you'll be asked

- **"Did AI tools help?"** Delivery compares AI-assisted pull requests with others from the same repo, month and size.
  Raw comparisons mislead: on public repos a 9-point gap all but disappears once compared like with like
  ([AI card](../../bench/accuracy/ai/README.md)). The result is an association, never a cause.
- **"How do we compare?"** Benchmarks are against similar public repos, with the sample size beside each.
- **"Can I see this per person?"** No. StackVitals names people only to route work (an owner, who acts next).

## Across several teams

Ask your platform team for the Portal's org view: every repo's figures added up, with the repos leading each
problem ([platform guide](platform.md)).
guides-platform:
You run GitHub for an org and want one view of every repo, owners that are real, standards people can see coming,
and a security review you can sign off.

## Roll it out

1. **Portal first.** Create a private repo (for example `portal`) and save the workflow from
   `stackvitals portal init` in it (`stackvitals portal check my-org` first says what your token can read (it uses your `gh auth login` or `GITHUB_TOKEN`)). With the built-in token it reads public repos; for private ones, an org
   owner creates a read-only org App (`stackvitals portal app-link my-org` opens GitHub's form filled in)
   ([modules](../modules.md#portal)).
2. **The suite per repo.** Each team runs `stackvitals init OWNER/REPO` ([quickstart](../quickstart.md)), which
   commits the workflow with that repo's CI workflows named and follows the first run. Private repos set `pages: artifact` (each run that
   changed the app uploads it as a download kept 7 days) or open the app with `stackvitals ui OWNER/REPO`.
3. **Settings as code.** `.github/stackvitals.toml` per repo; every setting, its default and the permission it needs
   are in [settings.md](../settings.md).

## What the Portal gives you

- **Owners, checked:** CODEOWNERS as GitHub reads it, teams with members, people still in the org.
- **Scorecards** (bronze, silver, gold) with evidence, your own rules in `portal.toml`, and `from = <date>` so a new
  rule shows what it would say before it counts.
- **Campaigns** with a date, a tracking issue and reminders; **required checks** for a level; **golden paths** that
  open a pull request with your standard files; a **docs index**; a **Backstage** export.
- **The org view:** totals and medians of what every repo published, with the five worst repos on each.

## Security and compliance

- [Threat model](../threat-model.md): each threat, what stops it, and the test that holds it.
- [Enterprise controls](../enterprise.md): SSO, permissions, audit log and data residency all come from GitHub.
- StackVitals' own workflows pin every action to a commit, and the release workflow signs releases with Sigstore and
  adds an SBOM; pin the Action itself to a release's commit SHA ([SECURITY.md](../../SECURITY.md)).
- [What leaves your repos](../privacy.md): every outside host the code can reach, each optional.

## Scale

For busy repos (2,000 CI runs a day), CI Health alone is estimated at under 40% of the built-in token's hourly limit;
their CI history keeps about four months under the default 250 MB cap ([scaling](../scaling.md)). Portal reads about 180 to 260 repos per run with the
built-in token and continues where it stopped.
